pronunciation.approximation: say-RAIN, stacked macron+acute on the final ē.
pronunciation.note: Greek Σειρήν carries the accent on the final syllable — Seirḗn — and the etymology is contested: folk tradition heard σεῖρα, "cord," for the binding song, while modern scholarship looks to Semitic or pre-Greek roots. The macron on the eta preserves the long vowel of the nominative.

domains.title: The Song that Knows
domains.subtitle: Knowledge, Enchantment, and the Bone-Strewn Meadow
domains.lead: Seirḗn is the most intelligent monster in the Odyssey: she does not promise pleasure but knowledge — "we know everything that happens on the fruitful earth." The Greeks feared her because her offer is exactly what the wise cannot refuse.

cards.name: The Song
cards.desc: Not seduction but information: the Sirens sing the Trojan War to the man who fought it.

cards.name: The Mast
cards.desc: Odysseus bound, crew deafened with wax — the original architecture of resisting temptation.

cards.name: Orpheus' Counter-Song
cards.desc: The Argonauts were saved not by wax but by art: Orpheus out-sang the Sirens themselves.

cards.name: Bird and Maiden
cards.desc: The Greek form — woman's head on a bird's body; the fishtail mermaid is a medieval graft.

symbols.name: The lyre
symbols.meaning: Song as the instrument of capture — art's dangerous edge

symbols.name: The meadow of bones
symbols.meaning: The flowering shore ringed with the rotting skins of the enchanted

symbols.name: The wax
symbols.meaning: Deliberate deafness — the technology of the will

mythology.lead: Daughters of the river-god Achelōos and a Muse — Melpomenē or Terpsichorē in the later accounts — the Seirḗnes unite the authority of water and the authority of song.

myths.title: Odyssey 12
myths.text: Kirkē warns Odysseus: the Sirens "enchant all who come near," and their island is heaped with bones. He has his crew plug their ears with wax and lash him to the mast. The Sirens hail him by name — they know his story — and promise that whoever hears them sails away "wiser." He strains at the ropes; the ship passes; the danger is measured in the distance of a song.

myths.title: Out-Sung by Orpheus
myths.text: Apollonius Rhodius sends the Argonauts past the same shore: one crewman, Boutēs, leaps overboard in surrender, but Orpheus strikes his lyre and drowns the enchantment in a nobler song. Later tradition completes the logic — defeated by Odysseus or Orpheus, the Sirens throw themselves into the sea and become rocks: a song that fails to bind has no reason to exist.

myths.title: The Lost Wings
myths.text: In Euripides' Helen and later lyric, the Sirens are mourners: they searched the world for the abducted Persephonē and were given — or kept — their wings for the search. It is the myth behind the monster: grief transformed into inquiry, the song that asks after the lost girl forever.

myths.title: Companions of Persephonē
myths.text: The fullest genealogy makes them the girlhood companions of Persephonē: they were playing with her in the meadow when Hádēs struck, and they asked the gods for wings to search the world for her. In Ovid's telling their transformation is their answer to failure — half bird, half maiden forever, still calling across the sea for the lost girl. The myth explains everything about them: the song that stops ships is a search that never ended, and the sailors it kills are drowned in someone else's grief.

lore.syncretism: Late antiquity moralized her: Christian writers made the Sirens the seductions of the world, the mast the cross. The Middle Ages merged her with the fish-tailed northern mermaid — the bird-maiden of Greece becoming the siren of romance — and French gave the world sirène, which is why modern alarm sirens and mermaids share a word. Kafka's parable "The Silence of the Sirens" gave her the last modern turn: a more fatal weapon than song is silence.
lore.culturalLegacy: "Siren song" is the fixed phrase for an irresistible, ruinous offer; "siren" became the alarm that itself enchants. Adorno and Horkheimer made Odysseus-at-the-mast the parable of the bourgeois self — pleasure permitted only under bondage — and feminist readings recover the Sirens as the suppressed voice of female knowledge. Ambulance sirens, film mermaids, and every warning that allures are her descendants.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Seirḗn is the patroness of dangerous knowledge — the truth that costs the listener his course. The Greeks' answer was not ignorance but engineering: hear the song, keep the ropes. Her question remains the sharpest in the Odyssey: if a voice offered to tell you everything, could you sail past it?

Her question has only sharpened in the age of the infinite song. Every feed is the meadow now — a voice that knows your name, your war, your wants, and promises wisdom if you only stop rowing. The Odyssey's answer was never ignorance: hear everything, keep the ropes, and let your crew row deaf through the meadow of bones. Attention is the last navigable strait, and she still sings on both shores of it.

Notice what the myth never does: it never silences them. The Greeks kept the song on their vases, their tombs, their stages — the danger preserved in full voice, ropes and all. That is the tradition's real instruction: do not destroy the enchantment, bind yourself honestly to your course, and let the singing continue. Some knowledge is only safe underway.
lore.archaeology: Greek art fixes her form early: bird-bodied, woman-headed, from the 7th century BCE — the famous Attic red-figure stamnos in the British Museum (ca. 475 BCE) shows Odysseus bound to the mast beneath three Sirens, the great birds with women's faces wheeling above his ship. South Italian funerary art made Sirens the musicians of the dead, carved on tombs of Campania and Apulia as mourning escorts. Odyssey-related localizations — the Sirenum scopuli off the Amalfi coast — are ancient tourism, reported already by Strabo.
